8.0.s.en: (1) The woman caught in the very act

8.0.0.en: "Jesus went unto the mount of Olives": St. John does not indicate why the Lord went to the Mount of Olives. But it can be inferred from what St. Luke said (Lk 6:12), that He used to go out to the mountain and spend the whole night in prayer. The Mount of Olives lies east of Jerusalem.

8.1.0.en: "Early in the morning": that is, the second day after the end of the feast. And He went to the Temple to complete His teaching of the crowds, and sat down like the great teachers of the Jews, speaking to them about the preaching of the Kingdom.

8.1.1.en: My beloved brother... do you not notice with me what the manner of life of the Lord Christ was?... There was no time to waste. After arduous service for four days at the feast with the crowds, and then a night spent in prayer, He returned to teaching once more... This is the positive work that all of us lack in our lives, for we squander much of our time on things that are of no use... while the other things, which remain profitable and are necessary for the salvation of our souls, we give nothing but crumbs...

8.1.2.en: Beloved... would that we remembered that for every moment and every minute we shall give an account...

8.2.0.en: The story of the adulterous woman is one of the famous stories, and St. John took care to record it. Before entering into its events, we note that the key to the whole story is in (v. 6), where it is made clear that the purpose and the motive were one thing: to entrap Jesus and to find a reason to accuse Him, regardless of the woman and her story. What happened can be summarized as follows.

8.2.1.en: (1) They had no need to ask Christ, for the Law is clear in (Lev 20:10) and (Deut 22:22) that the adulterer and the adulteress both are to be stoned to death, especially since this woman was "in the very act." What need was there, then, to ask Christ?

8.2.2.en: (2) They presented to Christ the text of what Moses said. Would He contradict the Law, and become a breaker and transgressor of it, exposed before the people? Or would He pass a sentence of stoning upon her, though He had no civil authority, since death sentences were the prerogative of the Roman state, which did not permit the death of an adulteress by stoning under Roman law? Consequently, if Christ declared that she should be stoned, He would become a transgressor against Caesar's authority; and this was the dilemma that the accusers had devised. (3) Cunning prevailed over them, and they wished to entrap the Lord, addressing Him as "Master," a very great title, limited to the class of recognized teachers of the Law (the Rabbis). So their use of the word "Master" did not mean that they respected Him, or that they meant it, but was for the purpose of entrapping Him.

8.3.0.en: "He stooped down, and with His finger wrote on the ground": He stooped down calmly, as though the matter did not concern Him.

8.3.1.en: This calm is a lesson for us in our conduct from the Lord Christ, for evil is not met with quick, agitated replies. He wanted to absorb their fury and their plot, and to lessen their seething against Him. Would that we learned how to meet plots with calm and prayer, before offering any opinion...

8.3.2.en: As for what Christ wrote on the ground, John did not mention it, and the Fathers who interpreted it differed over it. The following are some of the opinions:

8.3.3.en: (1) He may have written "Whoever has erred in one commandment has become a transgressor of all the commandments," as a preparation for what He would tell them, that they had no right to judge anyone.

8.3.4.en: (2) He may have written some of the commandments which most of them had broken, with the intention of rebuking them for the hardness of their hearts.

8.3.5.en: (3) He may have written what He had said before in the Sermon on the Mount, "Judge not, that ye be not judged..." (4) He may have written what He spoke, namely: "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her."

8.3.6.en: The Church accepts all these opinions by way of contemplation and inference, and there is no definitive opinion that can be adopted alone.

8.4.0.en: The insistence and the questioning continued, and the Lord broke off what He was writing and straightened up. His answer came as a depth of divine wisdom, against the cunning and malice of devils. For Christ neither acquitted the woman nor condemned her, but added to the Law the depth and spirit of the commandment: one who breaks the Law has no right to condemn another by the Law. So if there is none among you who is a breaker of the Law, let him begin by stoning her...

8.4.1.en: This is also what St. Paul said: "For wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things" (Rom 2:1).

8.4.2.en: And so the Lord gives us a beautiful new lesson in how wisdom delivers its possessor from plots. But we must first pray to the Holy Spirit, the Giver of this wisdom, and second be calm and unhurried before answering.

8.5.0.en: The Lord Jesus' stooping down this time was a truce that He gave as an opportunity for the crowd to depart, reflecting on what He had said, without a new confrontation. As for what He was writing, we have referred to it in (v. 6).

8.6.0.en: St. John portrays here how the few words of Christ were effective and at work in hearts and consciences. And how could they not be, since they were the living and powerful Word of God, piercing even to the dividing of soul and joints and bones? The response came first from the elders, because their spiritual perception was higher, then the young followed them, letting the stones fall from their hands, remembering only their own transgressions and sins. And the scene was emptied of everyone, except the Lord alone and the adulterous woman.

8.7.0.en: Here the Lord began to speak with the woman, who was in a state that would never have allowed her to begin to speak, because of her shame and embarrassment...

8.7.1.en: But is this not the heart of Christ, to whom we pray in the Litany of the Sick: "O hope of those who have no hope, and helper of those who have no helper, comfort of the fainthearted"?

8.7.2.en: It is a heart of love and forgiveness, and it always stretches out its hand to the brokenhearted.

8.7.3.en: And He began to ask her about the accusers who had departed, although He knew of their departure, but He wanted to spread reassurance in her. Those who wanted her dead no longer sought her. And when she answered Him, He said to her: even though I am the God who judges, and even though I am the only one who is without sin, I also do not condemn you. But go and sin no more. For God's forgiveness does not mean license and a return to sin, but it means that God's mercies open an opportunity for repentance before the sinner, who must make use of it.

8.7.4.en: My beloved brother... perhaps we may come out of this story, with all its events, with one important lesson, which is that we should not condemn anyone, placing before our eyes Christ's saying that if any one of us is without sin, let his brother condemn first... So let us cast far away the stones of condemnation that are in our hands, for we are under the very same judgment, and let us pray for our brothers instead of condemning them, that God may have mercy on us also together with them.

8.8.s.en: (2) Christ the light of the world

8.8.0.en: Here again the Lord connects His words with what He had said before, that He is the living water (ch. 7:38). Just as He cried out about Himself then, so today He cries out, presenting Himself as the light of the world, also using one of the rites and symbols of the feast, the rite of light. In the Temple, in the outer court, there were four very high pillars, and each pillar carried four wicks that were lit at the Feast of Tabernacles, giving a great light. This rite signified God, the light of the world, and was a remembrance of the pillar of fire that God sent in the wilderness to lead His people by night in the wilderness of Sinai. So Christ cries out once more, declaring Himself: "I am the light of the world." Note, dear reader, that when the talk was about the manna, Christ presented Himself as the true bread, the bread of life, and the living bread (ch. 6:32, 35, 48, 51). And now, the talk being about the light of the feast, He presents Himself as the true light of the world. It is as though Christ is saying that all the pale symbols of the past have today become a shining reality in the Son of Man, in His Incarnation, in which all the symbols were fulfilled. And let us note some spiritual meanings in these words:

8.8.1.en: (1) Because He is the light of the world: everything other than Him, or outside of Him, has become darkness.

8.8.2.en: (2) Because He is the light of the world: He has become the only source of guidance for the soul lost in sins.

8.8.3.en: (3) Because He is the light of the world: He has granted His children to have within them a light of life by which they distinguish things, reflecting His light to all who are around them.

8.8.4.en: (4) Although He is the light of the world: He left man the freedom to follow Him or not to follow Him by his own will.

8.8.5.en: And the Church, beloved, has taken care to remind her children always of all these meanings in the daily prayer of Prime in the Agpeya, for we read the first chapter of the Gospel of John, which describes Christ as the light that shone in the darkness. We also pray in the Psalms and the morning Midnight Praise: "O true Light, who enlightenest every man that cometh into the world." Would that you always remembered this attribute of your God, so that your soul may shine with His divine light...

8.9.0.en: The Pharisees relied on the fact that the Law of Moses requires two witnesses to establish a case, and does not accept a man's testimony about himself. By this they justified their refusal to accept Christ's thought, and His saying that He is the light of the world.

8.10.0.en: In (ch. 5:31), Christ says: "If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true...

8.10.1.en: There is another that beareth witness of me..." meaning the Father's witness to the Son.

8.10.2.en: But here, with the days of Christ's Incarnation drawing near and only a little time remaining, He began to declare Himself with power and clarity, and made clear that His witness about Himself is true, because He Himself is the Truth, and it is not for the darkness to judge the light. John the Baptist had already borne witness to me, and the Father likewise bears witness to me, and also my works. But now, I bear witness to myself, and my witness is true, and you will neither accept it nor understand it, because you do not comprehend the mystery of the Incarnation, so you do not know whence I came, and you do not know whither I go afterward, meaning His eternal existence in the bosom of the Father, and then His ascension to heaven.

8.11.0.en: "Ye judge after the flesh": it has two meanings:

8.11.1.en: The first meaning: you judge according to your fleshly desires and inclinations. This is because they condemned Christ and considered Him a liar when they said, "We do not accept your witness."

8.11.2.en: The second meaning: they judge according to their fleshly view of the person of Christ, and knowing His lineage and His earthly homeland. This is a limited view according to outward appearance, lacking the spiritual insight that perceives the reality of Christ's divine essence.

8.11.3.en: "I judge no man": this is because He did not come to judge the world, but to save it (ch. 3:17). And Christ demonstrated this also by not condemning the adulterous woman whom they brought to Him.

8.12.0.en: That is, even if I do not judge now, since the present mission is to offer salvation, judgment belongs to my divine attributes. And His judgment is true, because He is the Truth. And the Lord Christ returns once more to link Himself with the Father in the oneness of the divinity, for judgment is the right of God, and the Father has given it to the Son (ch. 5:22), who will judge everyone who does not accept the work of His salvation, or rejects His commandment and does not act upon it.

8.13.0.en: Christ presents to the Pharisees the answer to their objection about not accepting His witness in (v. 13): that even though His witness about Himself is true, there is One who bears witness and confirms it, namely the heavenly Father who sent Him, and gave Him as salvation for the world (Deut 17:6).

8.14.0.en: The Jews asked maliciously in order to entrap Christ, for when He spoke of His heavenly Father in (ch. 5:18), they sought to kill Him. And here too they wanted to catch Him in a word, but Christ did not answer them as to what they asked, but showed that the reason for their not knowing the Father was their ignorance of His own person, since He is the visible image of the invisible Father; and let us review a saying of Christ in another place: "If I had not done among them the works which none other man did, they had not had sin: but now have they both seen and hated both me and my Father" (ch. 15:24, 25).

8.15.0.en: The treasury is one of the places in the Temple, in the Court of the Women. The Lord used this place because it was the most crowded with people, owing to the offering of vows and the like. And despite the severity of Christ's words to the Jews, no one was able to seize Him, because He alone determines His hour, and not according to the opinion or counsel of any man.

8.15.1.en: O my God... perhaps the Jews had an excuse for their spiritual blindness and for not recognizing You. But what is my excuse, I who am anointed with the Holy Spirit? How ugly is my offense when I leave You, O true Light, and fall into the darkness of sin. Yes, I am without excuse. But I return and thank You, because You have placed in Your Church those who support me and raise me up, and who read over me the absolution of forgiveness, so that the eyes are opened again to the splendor of Your limitless light... O my God... do not let my knowledge of You be at the level of the mind and theories, but I want the knowledge of complete enlightenment, O true Light, who enlightenest every man that cometh into the world.

8.16.s.en: (3) The judgment of unbelief in Christ

8.16.0.en: The repeated dialogue returns once more, with Christ meaning one thing and the Jews understanding another. And verse 21 corresponds in its meaning to what came in (ch. 7:33-34), and the meaning is that you will die in the sin of unbelief in the Son, and you will seek and wait for an earthly messiah according to your own desire, and you will not find him. And because of your unbelief, you will not be able to enter the Kingdom of Heaven (v. 22). As for the Jews, with their usual mockery and closed spiritual vision, they did not understand the divine intention, but expressed their spiritual blindness and their hatred of Christ, saying that the only solution for understanding His words is that He is about to kill Himself, and that is the only place to which they cannot go, that is, "Hades."

8.17.0.en: The Lord Christ makes clear here the cause and the disease, and the difference between the words "I" and "you" in the previous verse, which is the difference between all that is heavenly and spiritual and what is earthly and temporal, tied to the glories of the world which I do not seek. And (v. 23) completes the meaning of (v. 14) of the same chapter: "I know whence I came, and whither I go," and both verses are a clear reference to Christ's Incarnation, His coming down from heaven, and His eternal divine nature. And Christ presents once more the cause of their destruction, which is their unbelief in Him!!!

8.17.1.en: My beloved Lord... Your conversation with the Jews has raised in me a perplexing and frightening question: am I earthly? Or am I heavenly? Can I be with You where You are, there in Your Father's house, or can I not? You have given me, freely, the grace of the heavenly birth in the sacrament of Baptism. But I still find that what is within me is inclined downward, toward the glories of the world and its falseness, forgetting the greatness of Your calling to me, to be from above as You are... My God, I fear for myself from myself, so do not allow me, my Lord, to slip downward, but draw me upward as You promised: "And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me," and make all the longing of my heart toward You alone.

8.18.0.en: The purpose of the Pharisees in their question, "Who art thou?" was not to seek clarification but to entrap. But Christ answered: "Even the same that I said unto you from the beginning"... that is, I have already declared who I am: "I am the bread which came down from heaven"... "I am the living water"... "I am the light of the world"... "I am He to whom my works bear witness"... "I am He to whom the Father bears witness"... and so on... that is, I am Christ, the Savior of the world. But is there anyone who understands, or accepts, or believes?!

8.19.0.en: "I have many things": Christ declares that He alone is the One who knows, and He alone is the Judge. If I speak concerning you of certain things, all of them are true, because I alone know what is in your hearts. And if I judge you, my judgment is true and just. But I also neither judge nor speak of myself, for I say what the Father also says, because I and the Father are one, and He is the One who sent me. And St. John adds in (v. 27) an explanation that Christ was referring to the Father here, without the Jews understanding His meaning.

8.20.0.en: Christ denies here any possibility of the Jews' recognizing Him before they lift Him up on the cross. Christ used the word "lifted up" to affirm the responsibility of His own, who rejected Him, for His crucifixion, and some of them would understand at His crucifixion, because of the events and signs that would accompany it, such as "the darkness" and "many coming out of the graves." The word "lifted up" also carries the humiliation of the cross, and the pain, and the glory of the exaltation accomplished through the redemption. And it is a very clear reference to the symbol of the bronze serpent that Moses lifted up on a pole so that everyone who looked at it would not die (Num 21:9). And Christ returns once more to affirm the nature of His unique, close relationship with the Father, in unity of knowledge and communion, and the Lord had pointed to this many times.

8.21.0.en: "He that sent me": that is, the Father, is with me and has not left me. And this reveals to us the mystery of the constant communion between the Father and the Son at the level of the one essence. For the Son, in His Incarnation, did not leave the bosom of the Father or depart from it, and likewise the Father also... And Christ concludes by adding a new theological truth, which is the union also at the level of will; for all that the Son does is the will of the Father, and all that the Father wills is done through the Son.

8.22.s.en: (4) The seed of Abraham and the concept of freedom

8.22.0.en: "Many believed on Him": but their faith was not sufficient, and is considered mere acceptance, as shown by Christ's urging them in verse 31 to continue in His word. And the coming verses of the same chapter show their swift turning against Christ.

8.22.1.en: "Ye shall know the truth": you will perceive who I am, for I am "the way, the truth, and the life" (ch. 14:6). And this Truth, that is, I, is the only One who frees from the slavery of lusts and sin, indeed the only Savior from the penalty of sin...

8.22.2.en: How sweet are Your titles, beloved Savior... for You are the Truth, and all that is besides You is falsehood. And You are Freedom, and all that is apart from You is a prison, even if with golden walls. How sweet it is that You free us from ourselves and our worn-out, perishing concerns, and call us to set out and enjoy the freedom of life with You, where all things become small, indeed cease to exist, so that nothing any longer troubles the soul, or imprisons it in its lusts or its base desires, far from You.

8.23.0.en: That is, we are children of Abraham the free man, who was never a slave to anyone, and therefore we are free... We note the following:

8.23.1.en: First: they did not understand what Christ meant spiritually, but turned to the political meaning of freedom, that they were not slaves to anyone, and their sonship to Abraham was the object of their fleshly boasting before the Gentiles.

8.23.2.en: Second: that, even on the level of material political understanding, they fell into a historical error, which is that they had in fact been enslaved to many kingdoms, such as Babylon and Assyria and the land of the Greeks, as well as the Roman rule contemporary with Christ. And because of this limited and mistaken understanding, they protested against Christ, how He could call them to freedom... without realizing the call of His salvation?!

8.24.0.en: "Verily, verily": a style of repetition for emphasis, which Christ used often. And the meaning here is: you do not understand what I meant by "the truth shall make you free." Therefore, in a new clarification, Christ confronts the Jews with what He meant, which is that every person who is unrepentant and lives the life of sin is a slave and not free, regardless of his lineage or affiliation or political description; for the measure of Baptism and freedom with God is unlike that of men, since it is either sin or repentance. Consequently, how many saints were imprisoned and exiled, yet the life of righteousness and repentance made them free... "A servant of sin": this word portrays for us the hideousness of the dominion of sin, as an evil master, controlling the will of man, who has no power or strength before this master. And sincere repentance, and the return to the bosom of God, are the way of true freedom from the yoke of this slavery.

8.25.0.en: As for the result, the slave enslaved to this evil master does not abide in the house for as long as sin is his master, for there is no place for slaves among sons. But the Son, that is, Christ, His abiding is a natural thing, for He is the heir of all His Father's house...

8.26.0.en: "If the Son therefore shall make you free": although Christ is the only source of true freedom, He put it in a conditional form: "If He shall make you free." And this condition does not relate to Christ's will in granting freedom, but relates to the Jews in their acceptance of this salvation or not; in other words: you have the true freedom granted by the Son, so will you accept it?

8.26.1.en: But as for the physical side (v. 37), I know that you are Abraham's seed. But this physical sonship has become very limited, and means nothing to God, as shown by your not accepting my word and believing in me, but instead of this, while I am the One who knows the thought of your hearts, you seek my death; and Christ repeated this saying in (ch. 7:19) regarding their desire to kill Him, and the phrase "my word hath no place in you" corresponds to what He said in (v. 31) "If ye continue in my word," and this means that Christ knew first that they had not continued and would not continue in His word!

8.27.0.en: "I speak that which I have seen with my Father" (see ch. 5:19-20) "and ye do": that is, Christ here denies their sonship to Abraham, and ascribes their sonship to Satan, for their seeking to kill Him is the will of Satan himself, and therefore, they have no right to claim that they are Abraham's children, as long as their work accords with the will of another father, who is the devil.

8.28.0.en: The Lord Christ draws our attention here to an important principle, which is that a man is not evaluated by what he claims about himself, but by the works that he does. For example, it is not enough to say: we are a Church that abounds with saints. But do we have the striving and the works of our holy fathers? Therefore, Christ denies to the Jews again their claim of sonship to Abraham, because of their works which contradict this affiliation. And the difference here is that Abraham believed and trusted in the word of God, and followed Him with all his heart. But those who claim to be his children reject the words of truth and life from the mouth of God Himself, and even seek to kill Him.

8.29.0.en: Since Christ denied to His hearers their sonship to Abraham, which greatly angered them because of their pride in this lineage, their reply came in two points:

8.29.1.en: The first: we are not born of fornication, that is, our genealogies are preserved back to Abraham, indeed to Adam, and we have not mingled with the Gentiles or intermarried with them; and the Jews always took pride in preserving the records of their genealogies by heart.

8.29.2.en: The second: they raised their sonship directly to God, who is higher than Abraham, and who is the one Father of us all.

8.29.3.en: Note: despite this boasting of false sonship, and the denial of the charge of fornication, the history of the Bible tells us that this people often went astray and committed fornication physically with the daughters of the Gentiles and intermarried with them, and also committed spiritual fornication by forsaking God, and worshipping the gods of the Gentiles on the high places and offering sacrifices to them (see Neh 13:23; Jer 3:6-10), which exposed them to the punishments of God, the hardest of which was their captivity and dispersion.

8.29.4.en: My beloved God... I fear that I may falsely believe of myself that I am called Your son, sharing with the Jews in what they ascribed to themselves. For if my life up to this moment is not free of sins, then do not quench Your Holy Spirit and the gift of life through Baptism within me. And if my sonship to You is deficient, let Your fatherhood to me remain perfect... and never leave me to myself.

8.30.s.en: (5) The children of the devil and their characteristics

8.30.0.en: Just as Christ denied the Jews' sonship to Abraham, He returns and denies their spiritual sonship to God, presenting the proof of this, which is the Jews' rejection of Christ Himself. And Christ presents Himself here, as He had also presented before, as the Word of God incarnate, for He is the One who proceeded forth from God, incarnate, and by the will of the Father for the salvation of mankind. So when the Jews reject the incarnate Christ, they reject God Himself. And Christ adds to His discourse another reason for the Jews' refusal to believe in Him, which is that the Jews heard Christ's words with their fleshly ears, and did not understand His meaning from the beginning, whereas they should have heard His discourse with their hearts, for the word of God is received by faith, and not by the limited mind or the fleshly ear.

8.31.0.en: This verse is considered one of the strongest confrontations in which the Lord Christ faced the Jews. The purpose was not to trample on their feelings, so much as to clear God and Abraham of this hard-hearted people. And by "the lusts of your father the devil" He meant here their desire to kill Him, for the wicked usually come together with Satan in one will, and so become children of his will. And the Lord continues His discourse describing Satan with the following characteristics: 1) "A murderer": that is, since evil entered his heart, Satan's only aim has been to destroy people and to lead them astray, for the perdition of their souls. Indeed, he is the only source of all conflicts and wars, and of inciting many to kill their brothers and their peoples. And Christ used the word "murderer" in the sense of a continual killer, to make clear that the destruction of people is the continuous work of Satan, indeed his only aim in all his works.

8.31.1.en: 2) "Abode not in the truth": when God created Satan, he was a great angel with a rank of leadership, that is, God created him in the light and the truth. But he, by his own will, did not abide in this truth, and sank down to all evil by his separation from God. See the story of the fall of Satan (Isa 14; Ezek 28:12-19).

8.31.2.en: 3) "A liar": one of the most important characteristics of Satan by which he leads people astray, as he led our first parents astray by his lie. And this characteristic passes on, by succession, to his children who bear his characteristics.

8.31.3.en: And this shows all of us the gravity of the sin of lying, which many do not take seriously, indeed do not consider a great sin, and which has become one of the necessities of daily life... Would that we examined ourselves, and remembered the fearful words of Christ on this subject.

8.32.0.en: The Lord Christ returns once more to the reason for the Jews' unbelief in His word: He speaks the truth, but they are the children of the liar, so they neither understand nor believe His words.

8.32.1.en: And here we take a new lesson from Christ, that the Christian man does not speak anything but the truth, regardless of whether his hearers believe it or not. Was it not so with the prophets whom the Jews killed? Was it not so also with our fathers the martyrs and saints who gave their lives for the sake of the truth?

8.33.0.en: The Lord presents here a strong proof of all that He had said before, and of His coming forth from the Father and His Incarnation. And He presented this proof in the form of a question to the Jews, namely: who of you convicteth me of one transgression, whether of the Law or of any other sin?

8.33.1.en: And this is evidence of the Lord's walk in righteousness, purity and meekness in His life, and a lesson for us also to walk as He walked, with exactness and continual examination of the soul. For a man is not what he claims for himself, but his conduct that conforms to the truth he proclaims, as was explained before (vv. 39-40).

8.34.0.en: Christ comes here to the end of a part of His dialogue with the Jews, in reply to verse 41: "We have one Father, even God." After He proved to them that they were not Abraham's children because of their works, and that they were children of Satan by their wicked will in attempting to kill Him, and by their lying, He comes to the end of this part, denying completely their sonship to God His Father, and presenting this as the reason for their not hearing His word and believing in Him.

8.35.s.en: (6) The accusation that Christ has a devil

8.35.0.en: The Jews found no charge to bring against Christ more severe than that He was a Samaritan, and the enmity between the two groups was great (see ch. 4). And they added also that He has a devil, as though they were replying to Him regarding what He had accused them of... and that out of their anger at what He had said about them. And they did not support this charge with anything, because they knew well that He was a Jew, and they had not found one sin in Him. Therefore, what the Jews said about Christ is counted as abuse and insult.

8.36.0.en: As for Christ, He was not occupied with defending His Jewish origin and lineage, but was concerned to repel and reject the second accusation, which touches the essence of His divinity and the holiness of His Father, expressing that the Jews' claim that He has a devil is an insult to the dignity of His heavenly Father which cannot be accepted or overlooked, because the One who is in Christ is the Father, so how can they say of the Father that He is a devil?!

8.37.0.en: "I seek not mine own glory": it is not my task to proclaim my glory, which is mine. For I came to bear humiliation and shame, and not to defend myself, for that is the task of my Father, who sees and examines everything, and who is jealous for my glory and seeks it, and who also judges everyone who has dishonored the glory of the only-begotten Son. And what Christ said here is a consolation to all His children who suffer persecution or insult for the sake of His name. For all that a man bears for the sake of Christ is counted as glory laid up for him, and also the just God judges the wicked according to His goodness and His just judgment.

8.38.0.en: Christ affirms a truth of the faith, which is that everyone who hears and keeps His commandment will not be hurt by the second death, but will have eternal life. And He had said the same meaning before in (ch. 5:24).

8.39.0.en: St. John returns and highlights the Jews' continued material, fleshly, literal understanding of Christ's words, instead of the spiritual understanding of them. And by their mistaken understanding they offered proof of the correctness of their previous accusation against Him that He has a devil. And the word "we know" means an assertion, and it resembles the expression of the high priest at the trial: "What further need have we of witnesses?" (Mt 26:65). And they continued to affirm their opinion that Abraham and all the prophets and fathers had died; so who are you that you should be given life and freedom from death? For they did not, of course, realize that He was speaking of release from eternal death, and not bodily death.

8.40.0.en: Verse 54 corresponds in its meaning to what came in (ch. 5:31), and adds that the Jews' claim that God is their Father did not bring them to the true knowledge of God, whom He knows with a personal knowledge, through the unity of nature and essence. And Christ affirms that if He claimed not to know the Father, He would be a liar like the Jews in their claim to know Him. And the proof that Christ offers of His knowledge of the Father is the keeping of His sayings and the obedience of His will, which are the simplest principles of the faith that the Jews did not do toward God Himself, and these are the cause of their judgment, and of their not recognizing the person of Christ.

8.40.1.en: Note, dear reader, that the Lord Christ still repeats that true faith is not that which is inherited, like the faith of the Jews, or that of which one boasts. But faith in the understanding of God is the keeping of His sayings and commandments and acting upon them in the life that we live... for how many people claim faith, and by their works deny it?!

8.41.0.en: This verse came as a reply to the Jews' insult to Christ in (v. 53) "Art thou greater than our father Abraham?"

8.41.1.en: As for the meaning: it is that He is truly greater than Abraham, for Abraham, with his standing among the Jews, was no more than a witness to the promises of God... and he, unlike you, believed the promise, and even desired to be a contemporary of the events of the Incarnation and redemption, and he saw them by faith, and believed and rejoiced, and exulted in the Spirit... And this is what St. Paul expressed in (Heb 11:13) when he said: "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them."

8.42.0.en: As usual, the Jews did not understand Christ's meaning, but interpreted His words as meaning that He had seen Abraham in the body. Therefore the Jews insulted Him again, saying: you have not reached the age of the elders, which is fifty years among the Jews, so how do you claim to have seen one who died two thousand years ago?! But Christ's answer carried the theological side in the declaration about Himself, and confirms what came in (ch. 1:1) "In the beginning was the Word." And the intended meaning: even if you are astonished and scoff at my being a contemporary of Abraham, the truth, which you also will not accept, is that I am before Abraham was; and this word "I am" is the very word that God used in presenting Himself to His people, when He said in (Ex 3:14) "Ehyeh" as His name, which means: "I am." So Christ here uses the name of God known among the Jews. And His saying "before Abraham was" is a clear reference to His eternal divinity.

8.43.0.en: The Jews considered what Christ said to be blasphemy, whose penalty is stoning. But because His hour had not yet come, He went out of the Temple, passed through and was hidden from their eyes, without their accomplishing their purpose of stoning Him. And so Christ reminds us again that, in many cases, it is wise to flee from anger, and not to confront it...
